title: How Students Use AI Feedback Matters: Experimental Evidence on Physics Achievement and Autonomy
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how different usage patterns of generative-AI-powered feedback affect high school students’ physics learning and autonomy. Rather than asking only whether AI feedback helps, the authors focus on whether effects differ depending on whether feedback is delivered through compulsory personalized recommendation or through more autonomous on-demand help, and whether these effects vary by students’ prior achievement level. The study is motivated by concern that AI may improve immediate task performance while also affecting students’ self-regulation and autonomy in different ways.

The researchers conducted two randomized controlled trials in a naturalistic school setting. In Experiment 1, Grade 10 students were individually randomized to receive personalized recommendations with AI-generated heuristic hints, personalized recommendations with conventional workbook answers/explanations, or no recommendations. In Experiment 2, students were randomized to an AI on-demand help system with full learner control, an AI help system with shared student-system control, or a control condition. Both interventions were paper-based because smart devices were restricted in school; students submitted physics errors or questions, which were scanned and processed by the system, and they received printed AI-generated hints, concept explanations, or related practice tasks. The AI hints were designed to be diagnostic, emotionally supportive, and heuristic rather than simply giving answers.

The population was high school students from a single school in southwest China, primarily Grade 10 physics learners. Across both experiments, the intervention lasted five weeks. Outcomes included objective academic achievement through school exam scores and self-reported self-regulated learning or learner autonomy questionnaires. The study also collected implementation and user-experience information through interviews and usage logs.

The main conclusion is that how students use AI feedback matters substantially. In Experiment 1, compulsory personalized recommendation with AI hints significantly improved achievement for lower-achieving students, while some conventional recommendation effects were weaker or negative for medium achievers; high achievers did not show achievement gains and showed declines in self-regulated learning. In Experiment 2, fully learner-controlled on-demand AI help significantly improved academic performance for high-achieving students without harming autonomy, whereas lower-achieving students exposed to on-demand AI help showed declines in autonomy. Overall, the paper argues that generative AI feedback is not uniformly beneficial: structured AI scaffolding may be more suitable for lower achievers, while autonomous AI help may better fit high achievers, and autonomy-related risks must be considered alongside achievement gains.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a strong K-12 experimental study with two randomized controlled trials in an authentic school setting and subgroup analyses, but it is a preprint under review rather than peer-reviewed, relies on school-specific implementation, and the provided text is incomplete for full results reporting and attrition assessment.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports medium-to-large subgroup effects on key outcomes, including physics achievement gains for some learners (d=0.673) and sizeable negative effects on autonomy for others (up to d=-0.549). Because impacts are substantively large though heterogeneous, the study fits blue impact magnitude while cautioning that effects are mixed rather than uniformly beneficial.

interventions.use_case: Generative-AI-powered personalized physics feedback for Grade 10 students, including heuristic solution hints, concept explanations, and student- or system-triggered on-demand help in a paper-mediated school workflow.
Algorithmic personalized recommendation of review problems based on students' homework errors and spaced repetition, with content delivered as recommended exercises and workbook explanations.
Non-generative comparator condition using recommended physics exercises plus publisher workbook answers/explanations, delivered through the same school-based recommendation workflow.

finding.finding_summary: Across two 5-week randomized experiments with high-school students in China (Experiment 1 n=121; Experiment 2 n=266; total n=387), generative-AI feedback had heterogeneous effects on physics achievement by achievement level and usage pattern. In compulsory personalized recommendation, low-achieving students improved when receiving AI heuristic hints (d=0.673, p<0.05), while no significant gain was reported for high achievers; in autonomous on-demand help, high-achieving students improved (d=0.378, p<0.05). The abstract also reports that medium-achieving students declined under a non-AI workbook-answer condition (d=-0.539, p<0.05), indicating the AI condition was not uniformly superior across all subgroups but showed targeted benefits depending on how help was used.
finding.measure: Standardized pre/post physics exam scores from school exams
finding.study_size: n=387 total; Experiment 1 n=121; Experiment 2 n=266
finding.effect_size: d=0.673 for low-achievers in compulsory AI-hint condition; d=0.378 for high-achievers in autonomous AI-help condition

finding.finding_summary: The study found that generative-AI feedback affected learner autonomy/self-regulated learning differently by subgroup and usage pattern. In Experiment 1, high-achieving students in the compulsory AI-feedback context showed a significant decline in self-regulated learning (d=-0.477, p<0.05) without achievement gains; in Experiment 2, autonomous AI help did not harm autonomy for high achievers but reduced autonomy among lower achievers (d=-0.383, p<0.05), especially on the technical-psychological dimension (d=-0.549, p<0.05). These results suggest autonomy costs when AI support is poorly matched to learner readiness or control structure.
finding.measure: SRL questionnaire in Experiment 1; four-dimension learner autonomy questionnaire in Experiment 2
finding.study_size: n=387 total; Experiment 1 n=121; Experiment 2 n=266

finding.finding_summary: The non-generative personalized recommendation comparator using workbook answers/explanations did not improve achievement overall and was associated with harm for some learners. In Experiment 1, low-achieving students showed a marginally significant positive effect under traditional recommendations (d=0.743, p=0.051), but medium-achieving students' performance significantly declined under workbook-answer support (abstract reports d=-0.539, p<0.05). This suggests conventional answer-based support was inconsistent and potentially counterproductive for some subgroups.
finding.measure: Standardized pre/post physics exam scores from school exams
